2.4 — Prefabs, Spawning & Playtesting

You have a working coin, spike and potion — singular. Games need dozens of each. Prefabs are the factory: build once, stamp many, change the master and every copy updates. Then, the professional ritual that runs the rest of your year: playtesting.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I spawn lots of the same object?”Outline only
Break It Down~10 minOutline only

I want a hundred coins in my level, and I am not dragging each one in by hand. The game should make them while it runs — and every one of them has to obey a setup I can still change in one place.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Name the thing that gets copiedwhat does this part do?Read: 2.1 and 2.3 — the prefabs you built there
  2. Hold a reference to that prefabwhat does this part do?Read: the GameObject row of this lesson's reference table
  3. Give the spawner a body to live onwhat does this part do?Read: 1.3 — Your First Script, and this lesson's Bug Hunt: Factory Faults
  4. Notice the key presswhat does this part do?Read: the Input.GetKeyDown row of this lesson's reference table
  5. Clone the prefab into the worldwhat does this part do?Read: the two Instantiate rows of this lesson's reference table
  6. Know what a clone is notwhat does this part do?Read: the callout info under this lesson's reference table

The split is the difference between a definition and an event. The prefab is the definition, the slot is your reference to it, and the clone call turns a definition into an object that exists for a few seconds. Only one part of the list is new code; the rest is file, field, and object placement you have done since 1.3.

The split is finished when every part names something you could point at in the editor: a file in Assets/Prefabs, a field in the Inspector, an object in the Hierarchy, a key, a method. A part you cannot point at is still a paragraph.

Your turn

Pick two of the parts above and say in one line what each one actually does.

This spawner runs inside Update(). Why does the key test have to be the one-frame version — and what would the Hierarchy look like at the end of a 90-minute class if it were not?

Prefabs: One Definition, Many Copies ~15 min

Step 1 — build the level. The Overworld scene ships with exactly one Coin instance, and no Spikes or Potions at all — you placed those by hand in 2.2 and 2.3. Now drag a handful of Coins out of Assets/Prefabs, plus several Spikes, plus the Potion prefab you built last lesson. Lay out something a player could actually walk around.

In the Hierarchy each one carries a blue cube icon: that marks a prefab instance — a stamped copy of a master. Select one and the Inspector shows the master's fields plus overrides, which is anything you have changed on this copy only.

Step 2 — change the master. Open the Spikes prefab itself (double-click it, or click Open Prefab). Now change something functional, not cosmetic: make its collider bigger, or adjust the trigger settings you chose in 2.2. Save and return to the scene — every spike in the scene updated at once, collider and all. That is the whole deal: one edit, every copy.

Now change one instance's position and scale in the scene. The Inspector shows that field in bold — that is an override. Master edits still propagate everywhere you did not override, which is exactly why an accidental override is so easy to miss.

Deleting a prefab's master file while copies live in scenes = missing-script chaos. The prefab IS the object's definition; the scene stores "a copy of that file, at this position." Treat master files like production code.

Master and Copy

  1. You changed the spike's collider on the prefab and every spike in the scene changed with it. If you had changed it on one instance instead, what would the other spikes look like — and where in the Inspector would you find the evidence of what you did?
  2. The Inspector prints an overridden field in bold. Why is an override so easy to forget you made?
  3. Deleting one prefab file breaks every copy in every scene at once, even though each copy is a separate object in the Hierarchy. What does that tell you about where a copy's definition actually lives?
Read the Docs: The Spawning API ~15 min

Objects do not have to be placed by hand. A game stamps them into existence while it runs — a coin from a broken crate, a bullet from a turret, a card from a deck. Unity does that with one method, and the table below is the whole of it. There is no code here on purpose: the API is given, and the script is yours to write.

APISignatureWhat you getWhat it costs
Instantiate (full form) Object Instantiate(Object original, Vector3 position, Quaternion rotation) Returns a reference to the clone. The copy arrives complete: every component the prefab carries, its tag, its colliders, its trigger settings. Three arguments, and the order is not negotiable — what to clone, where, what rotation. The clone belongs to this play session only: press Stop and it is gone, because the scene file was never written to.
Instantiate (short form) Object Instantiate(Object original) The shortest call. Clones at the prefab's own position and rotation. You get no say in where the clone lands, so two spawns in a row sit on top of each other and look like one object.
Quaternion.identity A Quaternion value, not a method "No rotation" — the clone aligns with the world axes. This is the constant to pass as the third argument. Nothing, apart from the vocabulary: it is the way to say "no rotation" in an API written for 3D, and it is the value a reader recognizes as deliberate.
Transform.position Vector3 (read and write) Where the object is in world space. Read the spawner's own position and you have a spawn point that travels with the object. World space, not local space. On a child object the two are different numbers, and a spawner parented under something else spawns in the wrong place if you mix them up.
Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode) bool Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode key) True on the single frame the key goes down — one clone per press, which is what a test key wants. It is a one-frame event. The version without Down is true on every frame the key is held, and holding a spawn key for one second is about sixty clones.
GameObject — as a type The type that holds a whole object, prefab asset and scene instance alike What you declare the Inspector slot as, so a designer can drag any prefab into it without touching code. The slot accepts any GameObject — and refuses anything that is not one, so a sprite dragged at it is rejected on the spot. What it cannot do is refuse the wrong prefab: put a Spikes prefab in the slot and it spawns spikes.
Object.name string (read and write) The name a clone carries in the Hierarchy — clones arrive named after the prefab with (Clone) appended, which is how you tell forty of them apart. Renaming is cosmetic. It changes nothing about what the object is or does.
Destroy(Object) void Destroy(Object obj) Removes a clone at the end of the frame — the cleanup you will need the moment spawned objects are meant to disappear. Final. Play-mode clones would vanish when you press Stop anyway, so this is for objects that have to go during play.
Three facts a signature cannot carry. First, the clone is a copy of the prefab asset, not of whatever the spawner happened to be looking at — which is why a spawned coin is collectable with no extra work: the tag and the trigger collider came with it. Second, a slot filled by dragging an instance out of the Hierarchy holds that scene object, not the asset, so it keeps stamping the old version after you edit the prefab. Third, spawned objects are events, not level: nothing you spawn is in the scene file, so nothing you spawn survives Play mode. Keeping a spawned object forever is a separate skill, and you meet it in Unit 3.

What the Clone Inherits

  1. A clone appears already carrying the prefab's tag, collider and trigger settings. What does that prove about what the clone call copies — the file, or the values currently sitting in an Inspector?
  2. You can clone from the prefab asset in Assets/Prefabs, or from a coin instance sitting in the Hierarchy. Both produce a clone. Which one still follows your edits next week, and what is the other one a snapshot of?
  3. The call hands you back a reference to the clone. Name one thing you could do with it later that you cannot do if you ignore it, and one reason an early spawner might ignore it on purpose.
  4. Press the spawn key thirty times in one place. What does the Hierarchy look like, and what does that say about why a real game reuses objects instead of building new ones forever?
Build Lab: ItemSpawner.cs ~25 min

This one is on you, and there is no code in this section. Attaching a script to an object is 1.3, a field that shows up in the Inspector is 2.1, and a prefab is 2.1 and 2.3 — the only genuinely new thing in this file is the clone call, and its shape is in the table above. The spec below names the file, the field, the method and the decisions; the rest is yours to write.

Architectural specification: the script and its slot.
  • What is the file called, and where does it live? Create it in Assets/Scripts, and name the class to match the file — what does Unity tell you if the two disagree?
  • A script on no object never runs. In the Overworld, create an empty GameObject (GameObject → Create Empty), name it something you will recognize, and attach the script to it. Why is a spawner its own object rather than another method on PlayerController — which of the two knows where the spawn should happen?
  • How do you expose a slot in the Inspector so a designer can drag any prefab in? What data type holds a reference to a prefab, and where does that field have to be declared so it survives from one frame to the next?
  • Where do you drag the prefab from — the Project window's Assets/Prefabs, or an instance in the Hierarchy? Say what each choice makes of your spawner, and which one still follows the master when you edit it next week.
  • The script compiles whether or not the slot is filled. What happens the moment you press the spawn key with nothing dragged in — and what would you look for in the Console?
Architectural specification: the spawn.
  • Which input function tests a single key press, and which key will you reserve for testing? What is the difference between it and the version that fires while a key is held — and what would the Hierarchy look like after one second of holding your spawn key?
  • Which three arguments does the clone call take, in order? Which of them is the constant meaning "no rotation"?
  • Where does the clone appear if you pass the spawner's own position? Where does it appear if you leave position out? Which do you want for a test key, and why?
  • Which prefabs in your project are ready to spawn right now — and what would you have to build first to spawn a third kind of object? (A prefab is a GameObject, and so is an instance of one. A sprite in the Project window is neither.)
  • The call hands you back a reference to the clone. What could you do with it later that you cannot do if you ignore it? If you ignore it, say why that is the right call today.
  • Everything this script makes exists only while the game is running. State the rule in one sentence: what do you have to do to put an object in a level permanently?

Press Play and press your key. Clones should appear in the Hierarchy with (Clone) after their name, and a spawned coin should be collectable exactly like the one you placed by hand. Then press Stop and confirm they are gone — and write down why, because that fact is the whole difference between a level and a spawn.

Playtest ~20 min

From today until June, this is the loop that makes every unit real: swap seats, play someone else's build, write what happened, fix the top three. Print the playtest sheet from Canvas (or copy its table into your journal):

ColumnWhat you write
What happenedFacts only: "died 4 times in the spike hall"
How it feltOne adjective per row: cheap, tense, confusing, satisfying
The fix I would tryOne concrete change: "move potion before the narrow hall"

The rules that make playtests honest: the tester plays and talks out loud but does not explain yet; the designer watches silently and takes notes; no defending, no arguing, no "you're holding it wrong." Then swap. Note that you will run this exact sheet on real data in 9.5, where the whole class's sheets become a dataset you will analyze — you are generating a dataset right now. Every jam this year ends with this ritual; the AP exam calls evaluating and refining (CRD-2) the same skills you are practicing by swapping seats.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain prefab master vs instance, and show an override in bold in the Inspector
  • Edit a master and see every instance update
  • Name the three arguments of Instantiate in order, and say what Quaternion.identity means
  • Explain why a spawned clone vanishes when you press Stop, and what that means for what belongs in a level
  • Choose between a prefab asset and a scene instance in an Inspector slot, and say what goes wrong with the wrong one
  • Run a silent playtest and turn notes into exactly one fix
